CD45RA is not simply a measure of total CD45/PTPRC expression; it reports the surface abundance of a specific CD45 isoform containing the variable exon 4–encoded “A” segment. In human lymphocytes, CD45RA is a canonical marker of naive/resting T cells and many B cells, whereas antigen-experienced or activated/memory-like T cells typically undergo CD45 isoform switching toward CD45RO through alternative splicing that skips variable exons, including exon 4. Therefore, in mixed primary cord blood mononuclear cells, cell-to-cell variation in anti-CD45RA CITE-seq signal should be strongly shaped by lymphocyte differentiation/activation state rather than only by total PTPRC mRNA abundance.

My single best hypothesis is: **variation in cell-surface CD45RA abundance across cord blood lymphocytes is primarily driven by activation-dependent alternative splicing of PTPRC, specifically TCR signaling–induced skipping of PTPRC exon 4 mediated by HNRNPL/HNRNPLL splicing repressors, converting cells from a CD45RA-high naive/resting state to a CD45RA-low/CD45RO-high activated or memory-like state.** In this model, CD45RA-high cells are resting naive T/B cells with high inclusion of PTPRC exon 4, while CD45RA-low cells have increased TCR/NFAT-dependent activity or expression of HNRNPL-family splicing regulators, leading to exon 4 exclusion and reduced surface CD45RA epitope expression.

This conclusion reflects **(a) established literature knowledge**: CD45 isoform switching is a well-known feature of T-cell activation and naive-to-memory differentiation, and HNRNPL has been implicated in regulating CD45/PTPRC alternative splicing. Supporting references include Trowbridge & Thomas, *Annu Rev Immunol* 1994, on CD45 isoforms and T-cell activation, and Oberdoerffer et al., *J Biol Chem* 2008, on HNRNPL regulation of CD45 alternative splicing.

A concrete test in this system would be to sort cord blood CD3+ T cells into CD45RA-ADT-high and CD45RA-ADT-low fractions, then perform isoform-specific RT-PCR or long-read/short-read splicing quantification across PTPRC variable exons to measure exon 4 inclusion. The prediction is that CD45RA-low cells will show reduced PTPRC exon 4 inclusion, increased CD45RO isoform expression, and higher HNRNPL/HNRNPLL activity or expression, even if total PTPRC mRNA is only modestly changed. Stimulating cord blood T cells with anti-CD3/CD28 should decrease surface CD45RA and increase exon 4 skipping, while HNRNPL knockdown, HNRNPLL inhibition, or blockade of TCR/calcineurin signaling should partially rescue exon 4 inclusion and maintain CD45RA surface abundance.
